## Exercise 4.4

**5. (e)** Find (i) $C=AB$, and (ii) $D=BA$, if
$$A=\begin{bmatrix}-2 \\ 4 \\ 7\end{bmatrix} \quad B=\begin{bmatrix}3 & 6 & -2\end{bmatrix}$$

<details class="solution">
<summary>Solution</summary>

$$C=AB=\begin{bmatrix}
-6 & -12 & 4 \\
12 & 24 & -8 \\
21 & 42 & -14
\end{bmatrix}_{3 \times 3} \qquad
D=BA=[3 \times (-2)+6 \times 4+(-2) \times 7]=[4]_{1 \times 1}$$

</details>

**7.** If the matrix $A$ in Example 5 had all its four elements nonzero, would $x^T A x$ still give a weighted sum of squares? Would the associative law still apply?

<details class="solution">
<summary>Solution</summary>

In Example 5, $x=\begin{bmatrix}x_{1} \\ x_{2}\end{bmatrix}$ and $A=\begin{bmatrix}a_{11} & 0 \\ 0 & a_{22}\end{bmatrix}$, in which case
$$x^T A x=\begin{bmatrix}x_{1} & x_{2}\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}a_{11} & 0 \\ 0 & a_{22}\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}x_{1} \\ x_{2}\end{bmatrix}
=\underbrace{a_{11} x_{1}^{2}+a_{22} x_{2}^{2}}_{\text{weighted sum of squares}}=\sum_{i=1}^{2} a_{i i} x_{i}^{2}$$

But if all four elements of $A$ are nonzero,
$$\begin{aligned}
x^T A x &= \begin{bmatrix}x_{1} & x_{2}\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}a_{11} & a_{12} \\ a_{21} & a_{22}\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}x_{1} \\ x_{2}\end{bmatrix} \\
&= a_{11} x_{1}^{2}+\left(a_{21}+a_{12}\right) x_{1} x_{2}+a_{22} x_{2}^{2}
\end{aligned}$$
which is no longer a weighted sum of squares. The associative law $\left(x^T A\right) x=x^T(A x)$ applies in both cases (after all, it's a law!) as all the products are possible.

</details>

## Exercise 4.5

**1.** Given
$$A=\begin{bmatrix}-1 & 5 & 7 \\ 0 & -2 & 4\end{bmatrix}, \quad b=\begin{bmatrix}9 \\ 6 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}, \quad x=\begin{bmatrix}x_1 \\ x_2\end{bmatrix},$$
calculate the following, indicating the dimension of the identity matrix used in each case.

a. $AI$

<details class="solution part">
<summary>Solution</summary>

$AI=\begin{bmatrix}-1 & 5 & 7 \\ 0 & -2 & 4\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}_{3 \times 3}=\begin{bmatrix}-1 & 5 & 7 \\ 0 & -2 & 4\end{bmatrix}=A$

</details>

b. $IA$

<details class="solution part">
<summary>Solution</summary>

$IA=\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}_{2 \times 2}\begin{bmatrix}-1 & 5 & 7 \\ 0 & -2 & 4\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}-1 & 5 & 7 \\ 0 & -2 & 4\end{bmatrix}=A$

</details>

c. $Ix$

<details class="solution part">
<summary>Solution</summary>

$Ix=\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}_{2 \times 2}\begin{bmatrix}x_{1} \\ x_{2}\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}x_{1} \\ x_{2}\end{bmatrix}=x$

</details>

d. $x^T I$

<details class="solution part">
<summary>Solution</summary>

$x^T I=\begin{bmatrix}x_{1} & x_{2}\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}_{2 \times 2}=\begin{bmatrix}x_{1} & x_{2}\end{bmatrix}=x^T$

</details>

**4.** Show that the diagonal matrix
$$\begin{bmatrix}
a_{11} & 0 & \cdots & 0 \\
0 & a_{22} & \cdots & 0 \\
\cdots & \cdots & \cdots & \cdots \\
0 & 0 & \cdots & a_{nn}
\end{bmatrix}$$
can be idempotent only if each diagonal element is either 1 or 0. How many different numerical idempotent diagonal matrices of dimension $n \times n$ can be constructed altogether from such a matrix?

<details class="solution">
<summary>Solution</summary>

Start with a $2 \times 2$ diagonal matrix:
$$\begin{bmatrix}a_{11} & 0 \\ 0 & a_{22}\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}a_{11} & 0 \\ 0 & a_{22}\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}a_{11}^{2} & 0 \\ 0 & a_{22}^{2}\end{bmatrix}$$

$x=x^{2}$ only for $x=0,1$, so $a_{11}$ and $a_{22}$ can each be 0 or 1. The $2 \times 2$ idempotent diagonal matrices are
$$\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}, \begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}, \begin{bmatrix}0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}, \begin{bmatrix}0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}$$

More generally, an $n \times n$ matrix allows $2^{n}$ such matrices: there are $n$ diagonal elements, each of which can take two values.

</details>

## Exercise 4.6

**2.** Given $A=\begin{bmatrix}0 & 4 \\ -1 & 3\end{bmatrix}, B=\begin{bmatrix}3 & -8 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}$, and $C=\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & 9 \\ 6 & 1 & 1\end{bmatrix}$, verify that

a. $(A+B)^T=A^T+B^T$

<details class="solution part">
<summary>Solution</summary>

$$A+B=\begin{bmatrix}3 & -4 \\ -1 & 4\end{bmatrix}, \text{ so } (A+B)^T = \begin{bmatrix}3 & -1 \\ -4 & 4\end{bmatrix}$$
$$A^T+B^T=\begin{bmatrix}0 & -1 \\ 4 & 3\end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix}3 & 0 \\ -8 & 1\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}3 & -1 \\ -4 & 4\end{bmatrix} \checkmark$$

</details>

b. $(AC)^T=C^T A^T$

<details class="solution part">
<summary>Solution</summary>

$$AC=\begin{bmatrix}0 & 4 \\ -1 & 3\end{bmatrix}_{2 \times 2}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & 9 \\ 6 & 1 & 1\end{bmatrix}_{2 \times 3}=\begin{bmatrix}24 & 4 & 4 \\ 17 & 3 & -6\end{bmatrix}_{2 \times 3}$$
$$C^T A^T=\begin{bmatrix}1 & 6 \\ 0 & 1 \\ 9 & 1\end{bmatrix}_{3 \times 2}\begin{bmatrix}0 & -1 \\ 4 & 3\end{bmatrix}_{2 \times 2}=\begin{bmatrix}24 & 17 \\ 4 & 3 \\ 4 & -6\end{bmatrix}_{3 \times 2}=(AC)^T \checkmark$$

</details>

## Exercise 5.1

**3.** Are the rows linearly independent in each of the following?

   a. $\begin{bmatrix}24 & 8 \\ 9 & -3\end{bmatrix}$
   b. $\begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{bmatrix}$
   c. $\begin{bmatrix}0 & 4 \\ 3 & 2\end{bmatrix}$
   d. $\begin{bmatrix}-1 & 5 \\ 2 & -10\end{bmatrix}$

<details class="solution">
<summary>Solution</summary>

a. Yes
b. Yes
c. Yes
d. No; the second row $= -2\; \times$ the first row.

</details>

**4.** Check whether the columns of each matrix in Prob. 3 are also linearly independent. Do you get the same answer as for row independence?

<details class="solution">
<summary>Solution</summary>

Yes, we get the same answer.

</details>
